about: The MySQL privileges that make an account an administrator of the SERVER rather than a user of a database. Written here rather than in a rule for one reason above the others: `SUPER` was deprecated in 8.0 and its powers split across a family of dynamic privileges, so a check that looks only for `SUPER` comes back empty on a correctly configured 8.4 server whose account is administrator in every way that matters. A list in code is a list nobody reconciles against the server; a list here carries its reason and is reconciled by a test that asks the server to accept every name. That reconciliation earned itself immediately: the first version of this file carried `SET_USER_ID`, which MySQL 8.4 refuses outright — it was split into SET_ANY_DEFINER and ALLOW_NONEXISTENT_DEFINER, and a rule reading the old name would have matched nothing on the engine this package targets while looking exactly like a rule with nothing to report.

entries.grants: Nearly every administrative action at once: killing other sessions, changing global variables, bypassing read_only, setting a routine's DEFINER to another account.
Changing any global system variable, which reaches the server's durability, replication and security settings alike.
Setting restricted session variables — including the ones that disable checks the server otherwise enforces on this connection.
Killing other accounts' sessions and connecting past max_connections and read_only — the ability to act on other users' work.
Persisting read-only variables, so a change survives a restart — the difference between altering the server now and altering it permanently.
Granting and revoking roles with WITH ADMIN OPTION, which reaches every privilege any role carries.
Setting a routine, view or trigger DEFINER to another account — the ability to have the server run code as somebody else. It is one half of what SET_USER_ID used to cover.
Creating an object whose DEFINER does not exist, which defers the question of whose privileges it runs with until somebody creates that account. The other half of the old SET_USER_ID.

Reading and writing files anywhere the server process can, as the server process — LOAD DATA INFILE and SELECT … INTO OUTFILE. The sharpest of the static ones: it turns database access into filesystem access on the database host, and it is the privilege an import tool asks for once and nobody narrows afterwards.

Seeing every session's currently executing statement, across all accounts. A statement is where credentials and personal data pass through in the clear, so this reads other tenants' traffic without touching their tables.
FLUSH of logs, caches, privileges and tables, plus RESET. It reaches the server's own bookkeeping, including re-reading the grant tables and taking a global read lock.
Stopping the server. Not a data privilege in any sense, and an application account holding it hands availability to whoever holds the credential.
Creating, dropping, renaming and re-authenticating ANY account on the server. An account with it can mint itself a second account, which makes every other restriction on the first one provisional.

Handing privileges on. Listed so the vocabulary is complete and marked unjudged here on purpose: it is a property OF a grant rather than an administrative power over the server, and it has its own rule. Two rules about one fact is the double report this catalog refuses.
